title: The Longest Window With Few Inversions

concept.title: Two pointers keep the window, and a Fenwick tree updates its inversion count when one number enters or leaves
body: An **inversion** in a window is a pair of positions `i < j` with `a[i] > a[j]`. In the window `3 1 2` there are two: `(3, 1)` and `(3, 2)`. Find the **longest window** (a block of neighbouring numbers) with at most `limit` inversions. Counting the inversions of every window from scratch is far too slow.

The inversion count of a window never decreases when the window grows to the right and never increases when it loses its first number. That is the monotonic property that makes **two pointers** work: extend the right end one step at a time, and while the count is above the limit, move the left end forward. All that is needed is the change of the count at each step, and a **Fenwick tree over the ranks of the values** in the window answers it.

body.code:
for hi in range(n):                              # the number a[hi] enters
    inv += (hi - lo) - bit_sum(t, rk[hi])        # numbers already in the window that are larger
    bit_add(t, rk[hi], 1)
    while inv > limit:                           # the number a[lo] leaves
        inv -= bit_sum(t, rk[lo] - 1)            # numbers after it in the window that are smaller
        bit_add(t, rk[lo], -1)
        lo += 1
    best = max(best, hi - lo + 1)

body: When `a[hi]` enters, the new inversions are the numbers in the window larger than it (the window size minus those that are at most it). When `a[lo]` leaves, the inversions it took part in are the smaller numbers that stand after it. Every number enters and leaves once: O(n log n) in total. A window with one number has no inversions, so the answer is at least 1.

statement: A list of `n` numbers is given. An **inversion** of a block of neighbouring numbers is a pair of positions `i < j` inside the block with `a[i] > a[j]` (equal numbers are not an inversion). Find the largest length of a block with at most `limit` inversions and print it.
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `limit`: the length of the list and the largest allowed number of inversions.
The second line has the `n` numbers of the list.
outputFormat: Print one number: the largest length of a block.

examples.note: The block 1 2 5 4 6 has only the inversion (5, 4). The blocks of length 6 and the block 3 1 2 5 4 have 3 inversions, which is too many: 5.

hints: If a block has few inversions, every smaller block inside it has at most as many.
Move the right end forward and the left end only when the count is above the limit.
Keep the window in a Fenwick tree over the ranks of the values to find how many inversions a number adds when it enters and removes when it leaves.

explanation: The right end of the window moves forward and the left end moves only while the inversion count is above the limit. A Fenwick tree over the ranks of the values gives the inversions added by a number that enters and removed by a number that leaves.
solution.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

def bit_add(t, i, x):
    n = len(t) - 1
    while i <= n:
        t[i] += x
        i += i & -i

def bit_sum(t, i):
    s = 0
    while i > 0:
        s += t[i]
        i -= i & -i
    return s

n, limit = map(int, input().split())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

vals = sorted(set(a))
rank = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(vals)}
rk = [rank[v] for v in a]
t = [0] * (len(vals) + 1)
inv = 0
lo = 0
best = 0
for hi in range(n):
    inv += (hi - lo) - bit_sum(t, rk[hi])
    bit_add(t, rk[hi], 1)
    while inv > limit:
        inv -= bit_sum(t, rk[lo] - 1)
        bit_add(t, rk[lo], -1)
        lo += 1
    best = max(best, hi - lo + 1)
print(best)
